topic: Blog authoring pipeline for a non-technical academic author (Dr. Satish Regonda, satishregonda.in): Google Docs → static site, evaluated against git-backed visual CMSes, Notion, Substack/Ghost/Hashnode/Buttondown, and raw Markdown-in-repo. Includes live API testing of the Google Docs export path.
key_findings: I EMPIRICALLY TESTED the Google Docs export path against the live Drive API (created throwaway Docs, exported, decoded, then trashed them). Everything below marked 'verified' is from actual bytes returned by Google on 2026-09-04, not documentation.

VERIFIED — Google's native `text/markdown` export is structurally excellent: headings, bold/italic, inline code, links, ordered + nested unordered lists, blockquotes, horizontal rules and GFM pipe tables (with `:---` / `---:` alignment markers) all survive intact. A Google Docs table exports as a clean GFM pipe table. This is far better than the folk wisdom suggests.

VERIFIED — Google's markdown exporter AGGRESSIVELY OVER-ESCAPES literal text. Typing `Inline math $\alpha = \beta^2$` in a Doc exports as `$\\alpha \= \\beta^2$`. Typing `[^1]` exports as `\[^1\]`. Observed escape set: `\ ` `*` `_` `[` `]` `#` `+` `-` `.` `<` `>` `=`. This silently destroys LaTeX, footnote syntax, and any code typed as prose. It is THE reason naive Docs→Markdown pipelines look broken.

VERIFIED FIX — a single left-to-right unescape pass, `re.sub(r'\\\\([\\\\`*_{}\\[\\]()#+\\-.!<>=|$&~^])', r'\\1', md)` plus collapsing Google's trailing `  \n` hard-breaks, recovers the author's original text BYTE-FOR-BYTE (I asserted equality against the source string and it passed). This ~3-line normalizer is the linchpin that makes the whole Google Docs path viable.

VERIFIED — images DO come out of the native markdown export, as reference-style definitions collected at the end of the file: `![Godavari hydrograph][image1]` in the body and `[image1]: <data:image/png;base64,iVBOR...>` at the bottom. ALT TEXT SURVIVES. A build script can decode these to real files with ~10 lines. Contradicts widespread claims that 'Google markdown export drops images'.

VERIFIED — the `application/zip` export is the better image path: it returns `.html` + `images/image1.png` as REAL BINARY FILES (no base64), with ``. Note the zip's HTML filename strips all non-alphanumerics from the doc title (`ZZ-test-image-export` → `ZZtestimageexport.html`), so never derive slugs from it.

VERIFIED — the `text/html` export does NOT escape literal text (LaTeX comes through clean as `$\alpha = \beta^2$`) but LOSES semantics: a code block becomes ``, a blockquote becomes an indented `

`, and the table is emitted with every row inside `` and an empty misplaced ``. It also rewrites EVERY outbound link through `https://www.google.com/url?q=&sa=D&source=editors&ust=...&usg=...`. Markdown export + unescape beats HTML export + parse.

VERIFIED — fenced code blocks DO NOT SURVIVE. A ```python fence round-tripped into plain paragraphs with `x \*\* 2  \# "quotes"`. Google Docs has no way to express a fence in the markdown export. Workaround: a 1×1 Google Docs table (the gd2md-html add-on already treats single-cell tables as code blocks) or a monospace-styled paragraph, detected by the sync script.
VERIFIED — headings can arrive emphasis-wrapped (`# **Figure test post**`) when the source heading carried bold. Strip emphasis that spans a whole heading.

`files.export` is HARD-CAPPED AT 10 MB (developers.google.com/workspace/drive/api/guides/manage-downloads). Base64 image inflation is ~33%, so an image-heavy post hits this fast. Escape hatches: `application/zip` (no base64 bloat) or the `files.download` long-running-operation method, which has no 10 MB limit.

Google Docs API `ImageProperties.contentUri` has a documented lifetime of only 30 MINUTES and is tagged to the requesting account — so the Docs API image route is a trap. Use the export routes above instead.

NETLIFY REVERSAL, CORRECTLY UNDERSTOOD: Netlify Identity is NOT deprecated (docs.netlify.com lists it as supported on all credit-based plans; the Decap maintainer confirmed 19 Aug 2026 that 'Netlify says it is staying'). But GIT GATEWAY *IS* deprecated — Netlify's own docs: 'While Git Gateway continues to function for sites that currently have it enabled, new Git Gateway configurations are not recommended… we will no longer fix bugs.' Git Gateway is precisely the piece that let a non-developer use Decap WITHOUT a GitHub account. So the classic Decap-for-clients setup is dead even though Identity survived.

Sveltia CMS is the strongest git-CMS in 2026 and is the right FALLBACK editor: drop-in Decap config compatibility, GitHub/GitLab/Gitea backends, first-class mobile support, and — critically — 'Sign In with Token' using a GitHub PAT requires ZERO backend and zero OAuth proxy (config is just `backend: {name: github, repo: owner/repo}`). Its docs claim ~750 Netlify/Decap issues solved and <24h bug-fix turnaround.

Pages CMS: MIT, ~4k stars, free hosted instance at app.pagescms.org, auth via a GitHub App, self-hostable but needs PostgreSQL + Node. Solid but adds a third-party hosted dependency and still requires the professor to hold a GitHub account.

TinaCMS is disqualified on price/complexity: free Tina Cloud tier is 2 users; EDITORIAL WORKFLOW (drafts/review/branch previews) is gated behind Team Plus at $49/mo. Self-hosting requires deploying a database (Vercel KV/Redis or MongoDB), an auth provider AND a GraphQL function.
Prose.io is effectively abandoned — its own docs say 'we do not offer support for Prose at this time', the image uploader is broken, and it is built on Backbone.js. Do not consider it.

Notion is disqualified on three counts: (1) rate limit is an average of 3 requests/second, 2,700 calls per 15 min per token, with no paid upgrade below Business/Enterprise; (2) `blocks.children` returns only first-level children so every nested level is independently paginated — one content-rich page can cost 30+ requests; (3) THE KILLER: every Notion-hosted file URL is an AWS S3 signed URL that EXPIRES IN ~1 HOUR, so any statically-built page referencing them 403s. Every image must be downloaded inside the build window. Payload limits: 1000 blocks / 500KB per request, 2000 chars per rich-text field.

Hashnode changed its pricing on 11 June 2026: the free plan is now one publication on a `hashnode.dev` subdomain, and CUSTOM DOMAINS, the GraphQL API, headless mode, webhooks and GitHub backup all moved behind Hashnode Pro at $5/mo (existing custom domains grandfathered). Headless-Hashnode is therefore no longer the free option it used to be. [Source is a third-party guide — treat the exact date as UNVERIFIED, the paywall shift as likely.]

Buttondown is the right newsletter layer IF one is wanted: native RSS-to-email that auto-sends on each new post, free to 100 subscribers, $9/mo to 1,000, no revenue cut. Compare Ghost(Pro) at $18/mo (Starter, 1,000 members) — Ghost is a whole CMS we don't need since we already own the frontend.

Astro's markdown config is MID-MIGRATION as of 2026: `markdown.remarkPlugins`, `markdown.rehypePlugins`, `markdown.gfm`, `markdown.smartypants` and `markdown.remarkRehype` are ALL marked 'Deprecated and will be removed in a future major version' in favour of a single `markdown.processor`. Write the config against `markdown.processor` now or we will be rewriting it within a year. `markdown.syntaxHighlight` defaults to `{ type: 'shiki', excludeLangs: ['math'] }` — the `excludeLangs: ['math']` exists specifically so math blocks pass through to KaTeX.

Drive push notifications are NOT a good trigger: a `files.watch` channel maxes out at 86,400s (1 day) and `changes.watch` at 604,800s (1 week), with no auto-renewal and a mandatory publicly-reachable HTTPS endpoint with a valid cert. Renewing a channel forever is more fragile than polling.

GitHub Actions `schedule` has a 5-minute minimum, 'can be delayed during periods of high loads… the start of every hour' (so never use `0 * * * *`), and — the trap — scheduled workflows in PUBLIC repos are AUTOMATICALLY DISABLED after 60 days with no repository activity. A blog the professor posts to twice a year will silently stop syncing. Keep the content repo PRIVATE, or add a keepalive.

Apps Script quotas make a 'Publish' button trivially cheap: `UrlFetchApp` allows 20,000 calls/day on consumer accounts and 100,000/day on Google Workspace, 50 MB per response, 6 min per execution. GitHub's `repository_dispatch` accepts a `client_payload` up to 65,535 chars.

GitHub Contents API (`PUT /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}`) takes base64 `content` + `message` + the existing blob `sha` on update; full feature support only up to 1 MB per file, raw/object media types 1–100 MB, nothing above 100 MB. Fine for markdown; use git (not the API) for image commits.

Cloudflare Pages free tier: 500 builds/month, 20-min build timeout, 20,000 files per site, 25 MiB max per asset, 100 custom domains. For a site that redeploys a handful of times a month this is permanently free and comfortably within limits.
recommendations: PRIMARY PIPELINE — 'Drive folder is the status flag.' Create in his Drive: `Website/Blog/Drafts/`, `Website/Blog/Published/`, `Website/Blog/Retired/`, `Website/Blog/data/`. He writes in Drafts. TO PUBLISH HE DRAGS THE DOC INTO `Published/`. That is the whole interface. Reject the Sheet-with-status-column (a second place to edit, and it desynchronises the moment a Doc is renamed or deleted) and reject the filename convention (`PUBLISH: …` is invisible, typo-prone, and pollutes the title we want to use).

METADATA comes from a 2-column Google Docs table titled 'Post settings' as the FIRST element of every Doc, with rows: Summary, Tags, Cover image, Slug (optional), Date (optional). Use a TABLE, not a `key: value` block — verified that Docs tables export as clean GFM pipe tables, and a table is visually obvious and cannot be broken by pressing Enter. The sync parses the first pipe-table, lifts it into frontmatter, and deletes it from the body.

SLUG AND DATE ARE STAMPED ONCE, NEVER RECOMPUTED. Keep `src/content/blog/_registry.json` in the repo keyed by Drive `fileId` → `{slug, pubDate, contentHash}`. First time a Doc appears in Published/, the pipeline slugifies the title and stamps today's date, then writes them to the registry. After that, renaming the Doc changes the displayed title but NOT the URL. This single decision eliminates the entire class of 'he edited the post and the URL changed and Google lost it' failures.

SYNC JOB: a `sync-blog.yml` GitHub Action on `schedule: '*/15 * * * *'` (never `0 * * * *` — that's the congested slot) plus `workflow_dispatch` plus `repository_dispatch`. Steps: authenticate to Drive as a service account → `files.list` the Published folder (`fields=files(id,name,createdTime,modifiedTime)`, add `supportsAllDrives=true` if it's a shared drive) → `files.export` each as `text/markdown` → normalize → write → `astro build` → ONLY IF THE BUILD PASSES, commit and push to `main`. Deploy time: ≤15 min unattended, ~2 min if he uses the button.

THE NORMALIZER, in this exact order — this is the part everyone gets wrong: (1) split off the trailing `[imageN]: <data:...>` reference definitions and decode them to real files under `src/content/blog/<slug>/`; (2) run the single-pass unescape over the body; (3) re-escape any line that NOW begins with `#`, `>`, `|`, `-`, `*` or `1.` but did not before (guards the one false-positive case: a professor literally typing a line starting with '#'); (4) collapse `/ {2,}\n/` → `\n`; (5) unwrap `google.com/url?q=` link redirects; (6) strip whole-heading emphasis (`# **Title**` → `# Title`); (7) promote an all-italic paragraph immediately following an image into a `<figcaption>`.

'PUBLISH NOW' BUTTON: bind an Apps Script to the Doc (`onOpen` adds a menu 'Website → Publish this post') that POSTs `repository_dispatch` to GitHub with a fine-grained PAT in Script Properties. Under 30 lines, one authorization prompt, and it collapses the 15-minute wait to ~90 seconds. RISK: iith.ac.in is a Google Workspace domain and an admin may block Apps Script external requests or third-party sharing — so the 15-minute poll MUST work standalone, with the button as pure convenience.

IF THE WORKSPACE ADMIN BLOCKS SERVICE-ACCOUNT SHARING (a real possibility at an Indian institute), swap the Drive auth for an Apps Script Web App that HE deploys under his own account, which returns the exported markdown as JSON to a shared-secret-authenticated GET from the Action. Zero service accounts, zero external sharing, zero admin tickets. Design the sync script with the fetcher behind an interface so this swap is a one-file change.

FAILURE HANDLING — never let a bad post break the live site. The build runs BEFORE the commit, so a malformed Doc simply produces no commit. On failure the Action opens (or updates) a GitHub Issue titled 'Could not publish: <Doc name>' AND emails him one plain-English sentence ('The post "Monsoon onset" could not be published — the Post settings table is missing a Summary row. Nothing on the website has changed.'). Silent failure is the only unacceptable outcome.

TYPO AFTER PUBLISHING: he edits the Doc. Nothing else. The next sync sees a changed content hash, rewrites the markdown, keeps slug + pubDate from the registry, and sets `updatedDate`. Render 'Updated 14 March 2026' under the byline only when `updatedDate > pubDate + 24h`, so fixing a comma doesn't shout at readers.

UNPUBLISHING: he drags the Doc to `Retired/`. The sync sees a registry entry with no live Doc and sets `draft: true` — it NEVER deletes the markdown file. Emit a 410 stub or a redirect. Treat 'the Doc vanished' as a possible ACCIDENT, not an instruction to destroy content.

DRAFTS ARE PRIVATE BY CONSTRUCTION: the `Drafts/` folder is simply never read. There is no preview URL, no `?draft=1` param, no noindex page to leak. If he later wants a shareable preview, add a `Preview/` folder that builds a `preview` branch to `preview.satishregonda.in` behind Cloudflare Access (email OTP to his address) with `X-Robots-Tag: noindex`. Phase 2 only.

IMAGES: the sync writes originals into `src/content/blog/<slug>/`, downscaling anything wider than 2000px and re-encoding to WebP q82 BEFORE committing (otherwise the repo accumulates 8 MB phone photos). Astro's `astro:assets` + sharp then emits AVIF/WebP with srcset at build. Switch that post to the `application/zip` export automatically if the base64 markdown export exceeds ~7 MB, to stay under the hard 10 MB `files.export` cap.

RSS: `@astrojs/rss` at `/rss.xml`, `site` set in `astro.config`, full post HTML in the `content` key run through `sanitize-html`, image/link paths absolutised. Add `<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml">` in the head and a visible RSS link in the footer — academics still use readers.

NEWSLETTER: yes, but as PHASE 2 and as a consumer of our RSS, not as the home of the writing. Buttondown RSS-to-email (free ≤100 subs, $9/mo ≤1,000, no revenue cut). Do NOT host the blog on Substack — it surrenders the domain, the typography and the canonical URL, and Substack's chrome is instantly recognisable as a template, which directly contradicts the 'must not read as generic' brief. Cross-post at most, always with `rel=canonical` back to satishregonda.in.

STANDING FALLBACK EDITOR: install Sveltia CMS at `/admin` from day one, configured `backend: {name: github, repo: <owner>/<repo>}` with PAT sign-in. It needs no OAuth proxy, no backend, no Netlify, and works on an iPad. Cost to keep: one config file. If Google ever changes the export format mid-trip, he can still fix a live post from a phone.

CONTENT ERGONOMICS — give him a ONE-PAGE house-style card, not a manual: (a) Headings via the Docs style menu, never bold text. (b) Figure = insert image, then one all-italic line under it = the caption; fill the image's Alt text field (verified it survives). (c) Equations = type LaTeX between `$…$` or `$$…$$` as plain text — NEVER use Insert → Equation, which the gd2md-html add-on explicitly cannot convert. (d) Footnotes = `[^1]` inline, `[^1]: source` at the end. (e) Code = put it in a 1×1 table with `lang: python` as the first line. (f) Tables = normal Docs tables. (g) Charts/maps = a lone paragraph `::chart: godavari-2024.csv` or `::embed: <url>`, with the CSV in `Blog/data/`; keep the directive vocabulary to three or four, ever.

MANDATORY ONE-TIME DOCS SETTING: in Tools → Preferences, turn OFF 'Use smart quotes' and the `--` → em-dash automatic substitution, so LaTeX and code survive typing. Astro applies smartypants at render time anyway, so his prose still gets proper curly quotes on the site. [Exact 2026 menu wording UNVERIFIED — confirm in his account during setup.]

HOSTING: Cloudflare Pages, content repo PRIVATE (this also dodges the 60-day scheduled-workflow auto-disable that would silently kill an infrequently-updated public repo). 500 builds/month is ~16× headroom for this publishing cadence.

DO NOT BUILD A PREVIEW/APPROVAL STEP FOR HIM. No PR to review, no 'ready for review' state, no staging URL to check. Every review gate is a step a non-technical author will not complete, and the post will sit in limbo. The Doc IS the preview; the guard rail is that a failing build never reaches production.

## 0. Method — this was tested, not just read I created three throwaway Google Docs via the Drive connector on 2026-09-04, exported each through the real Drive export endpoints as `text/markdown`, `text/html` and `application/zip`, decoded the base64 responses locally, and then trashed all five test files. Every "VERIFIED" claim below is from those bytes. Scratchpad artefacts are at `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-divyanshpandey-Desktop-Projects-Satish-Portfolio/0a1055f9-5c56-40cc-9342-e71706b18fa9/scratchpad/`. --- ## 1. Google Docs as the writing surface — stress-tested ### 1.1 What the export endpoints actually are Drive `files.export` supports for a Google Doc (per developers.google.com/workspace/drive/api/guides/ref-export-formats): | MIME | Extension | Notes | |---|---|---| | `text/markdown` | `.md` | shipped July 2024 | | `text/html` | `.html` | images inlined as base64 data URLs | | `application/zip` | `.zip` | HTML + `images/` folder of real binaries | | `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document` | `.docx` | | | `application/pdf`, `application/epub+zip`, `.odt`, `.rtf`, `.txt` | | | There is also an unauthenticated URL form for link-shared docs: `https://docs.google.com/document/d/{id}/export?format=markdown`. Convenient but requires the Doc be world-readable — unacceptable for drafts. Use the authenticated API. **Hard cap: `files.export` is limited to 10 MB.** Above that, use `exportLinks` or the `files.download` long-running-operation method. ### 1.2 Structural fidelity — much better than reputation Input Doc → `text/markdown` output, verbatim: ``` # Monsoon onset and reservoir inflow Some *italic*, **bold**, and `inline code`. A [link](https://example.org/a?b=c&d=e). ## Section two 1. First item 2. Second item - nested bullet - another > > A blockquote line. | Basin | Area (km2) | Q | | :---- | ----: | :---- | | Godavari | 312812 | 3.2 | | Krishna | 258948 | 1.9 | ``` Headings ✓, emphasis ✓, inline code ✓, links ✓ (unwrapped, real URL, query string intact), ordered + nested unordered lists ✓, blockquote ✓ (with a spurious leading `> ` line), GFM tables with alignment ✓, `---` rule ✓. ### 1.3 The escaping problem — the real blocker Same document, the parts that were **plain literal text**: ``` def q(x): return x \*\* 2 \# "quotes" and \-- dashes Inline math $\\alpha \= \\beta^2$ and a display block: $$ Q \= C i A $$ ``` And an isolated test on a doc built purely from plain text: ``` Inline math $\\alpha \= \\beta^2$ here. A footnote marker and a URL https://example.org/x\_y\_z and file\_name\_with\_underscores. Stars \* and 2\*3 \= 6 and a hash \# tag and a plus \+ sign. An em dash \-- and "double quotes" and 'single quotes'. A\[1\] bracket and 5 \< 10 \> 3\. ``` Observed escape set: `\` `*` `_` `[` `]` `#` `+` `-` `.` `<` `>` `=`. Consequences, concretely: - `$\alpha = \beta^2$` → `$\\alpha \= \\beta^2$`. KaTeX reads `\\` as a line break and `\=` as an unknown control sequence. Math is destroyed. - `[^1]` → `\[^1\]`. Footnotes are destroyed. - URLs with underscores get `\_` (most renderers cope, but it's noise). The escaping is **context-sensitive on provenance**: a Doc created by *importing* markdown exported `[^1]` **unescaped**, while a Doc where the same text was literal plain text exported it as `\[^1\]`. So you cannot rely on "it worked once". ### 1.4 The fix — validated ```python ESC = r"\\`*_{}[]()#+-.!<>=|$&~^" md = re.sub(r"\\([" + re.escape(ESC) + r"])", r"\1", md) md = re.sub(r"[ ]{2,}\n", "\n", md) # Google's hard-break double-spaces ``` I asserted the output against the original source string: **exact match, True.** Every backslash in Google's output is an escape it inserted, so a single left-to-right pass is provably lossless. One false positive to guard: if he types a line whose first character is genuinely `#`, Google emits `\#` and the unescape promotes it to a heading. Mitigation: after unescaping, re-escape line-initial `#`/`>`/`|`/`-`/`*`/`1.` on lines that were escaped before the pass. ### 1.5 Images — the pleasant surprise Native markdown export of a Doc containing one image with alt text: ``` # **Figure test post** Intro paragraph before the figure. ![Godavari hydrograph][image1] *Figure 1\. Observed vs simulated flow.* Text after. [image1]: ``` - Images ARE present, as reference-style definitions appended at the end. - **Alt text survives** into markdown alt text. - Extraction is ~10 lines: regex the `[imageN]: ]+)>` definitions, `base64.b64decode`, write `imageN.png`, rewrite `![alt][imageN]` → `![alt](./imageN.png)`. - Note `Figure 1\.` — the escaped period, again fixed by the normalizer. - Google **re-encodes** the image server-side (the returned bytes differed from what I uploaded), so don't expect byte-identical originals. - Base64 inflates ~33%. Combined with the 10 MB export cap, a post with a handful of full-resolution figures will hit it. Zip export of the same Doc: ``` ZIP ENTRIES: ['ZZtestimageexportsatishsite.html', 'images/image1.png']

Figure test post

Intro paragraph before the figure.

Figure 1. Observed vs simulated flow.

``` Real PNG (`b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n'` magic confirmed), no base64 bloat, alt text preserved, and the literal text is **unescaped**. Note the HTML filename is the doc title with non-alphanumerics stripped. ### 1.6 HTML export — good text, bad semantics From `text/html` on the structured test doc: - LaTeX comes through clean: `Inline math $\alpha = \beta^2$ and a display block:` and `$$ Q = C i A $$`. - Code becomes `inline code` — recoverable only by sniffing the font family. - Blockquote becomes `

` — indistinguishable from an indented paragraph. - Table is emitted with **every row inside ``** and an empty, misplaced ``. - Headings carry Google's own anchors: `id="h.a8a6s9mb95mk"` — must be re-slugged. - **Every outbound link is rewritten through a Google redirect**: `href="https://www.google.com/url?q=https://example.org/a?b%3Dc%26d%3De&sa=D&source=editors&ust=1788525647793945&usg=AOvVaw26GcsuFpTkN9-73UFNxM5B"`. Must be unwrapped. - Imports a webfont: `@import url(https://themes.googleusercontent.com/fonts/css?kit=...)`. **Verdict: markdown export + unescape is strictly better than HTML export + parse.** Keep the zip path as an image-heavy fallback. ### 1.7 The "publish this draft" signal — three options compared | Signal | Discoverability | Failure modes | Verdict | |---|---|---|---| | **Drive folder `Published/`** | Perfect — he drags a file | Almost none. Accidental move is recoverable. | **Chosen** | | Sheet row with status column | Good | Two sources of truth. Row exists / Doc deleted. Typo'd fileId. Duplicate slugs. Requires copying doc IDs. | Reject | | Filename convention (`PUBLISH: …`) | Poor — invisible state | Typos, case, trailing spaces. Pollutes the title. | Reject | The Sheet is right for *tabular* content (publications, students, alumni) and wrong for *documents*. Don't let consistency-with-the-rest-of-the-site drag the blog into a Sheet. ### 1.8 Triggering - **Drive push notifications: rejected.** `files.watch` channels max at 86,400s and `changes.watch` at 604,800s, default 3,600s, no auto-renewal, and require a publicly-reachable HTTPS endpoint with a valid non-self-signed cert. You'd be maintaining a renewal cron to avoid a poll — strictly worse. - **GitHub Actions `schedule`: chosen**, `*/15 * * * *`. Minimum interval is 5 min. Docs warn the event "can be delayed during periods of high loads… the start of every hour", so avoid `0 * * * *`. **Public repos get scheduled workflows auto-disabled after 60 days of no repository activity** — keep the repo private. - **`repository_dispatch` from Apps Script: chosen as the impatience button.** Apps Script `UrlFetchApp` allows 20,000 calls/day (consumer) / 100,000/day (Workspace), 50 MB per response, 6 min per execution. `repository_dispatch` accepts `client_payload` up to 10 top-level keys / 65,535 chars. ### 1.9 Converter landscape (if we didn't roll our own) - **Docs to Markdown (gd2md-html)**, Bean Road Communications — free, 1M+ installs, 175 reviews, last updated **28 Jan 2026**. Converts footnotes to standard markdown footnotes; tables to HTML (with merged row/col support); **single-cell tables become code blocks**; automatically straightens smart quotes inside code blocks; Google Docs *equations* raise an alert requiring manual MathJax conversion; images become placeholders you must move yourself; explicitly "does not preserve colors and styles". - **Docs to Markdown Pro** — same lineage, adds front-matter generation, one-click Git push with automatic image upload and path rewriting, TOC conversion, WCAG checks. $49/yr Personal (500 conversions, 100 git pushes, 1 repo) / $119/yr Business. **This is the buy-not-build fallback** if we ever want to retire the custom sync. - **Mr0grog/google-docs-to-markdown** — Remark/Rehype-based, BSD, but webapp-only (no CLI/library), so not automatable. --- ## 2. Git-backed visual CMSes — 2026 status | | Auth reality | Backend needed | Drafts | Media | Mobile | Risk | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Decap** | Git Gateway **deprecated by Netlify** | Netlify Identity (alive) + Git Gateway (dying) | editorial workflow | basic | poor | High — unpatched Sept-2025 XSS reported; slow releases | | **Sveltia** | **PAT sign-in, zero setup**; or own Cloudflare Worker OAuth client; or reuse a Decap OAuth client | **none** | supported | DAM + Unsplash/Pexels/Pixabay | **first-class** | Low, but single-maintainer | | **Pages CMS** | GitHub App | free hosted app.pagescms.org, or self-host w/ PostgreSQL+Node | yes | yes | ok | Low-med | | **TinaCMS** | Tina Cloud | Cloud, or self-host DB+auth+GraphQL | **$49/mo tier** | yes | ok | Cost/complexity | | **Keystatic** | GitHub App / local | none for local | limited | yes | ok | Single-agency dependency | | **Prose.io** | GitHub OAuth | none | no | **broken** | no | Dead | **The Netlify story, precisely.** Netlify Identity was announced as deprecated, then **reversed** — docs.netlify.com now lists Identity as supported on all credit-based plans, and the Decap maintainer confirmed on 19 Aug 2026 that "Netlify Identity is not deprecated anymore." But **Git Gateway is separately and still deprecated**, quoting Netlify's docs verbatim: > "Git Gateway is deprecated. While Git Gateway continues to function for sites that currently have it enabled, new Git Gateway configurations are not recommended. While we will keep fixing any major security issues that arise, we will no longer fix bugs in the functionality of Git Gateway." No end-of-support date, no migration path offered. Since Git Gateway was the *only* way a person without a GitHub account could commit through Decap, the client-friendly Decap setup is effectively over. DecapBridge (free ≤3 sites / 10 collaborators, $9/mo Pro, $199 lifetime, Google/Microsoft/password login) exists to fill that hole, but it's a young single-purpose SaaS to depend on. Sveltia's PAT flow is the quiet winner for our purposes — config is literally: ```yaml backend: name: github repo: owner/repo ``` and the user clicks "Sign In with Token", generates a PAT from a provided link, pastes it; the token stays in browser storage. No Worker, no OAuth app, no Netlify. Note: Sveltia's introduction docs state plainly that it "does not have a built-in user authentication system. Instead, it relies on the Git backend for user authentication and access control" — so the professor still needs a GitHub account. That's fine for a fallback editor; it's why it isn't the primary. --- ## 3. Notion — rejected, with the numbers - **Rate limit**: "an average of three requests per second, with some bursts"; ~2,700 calls / 15 min per token; workspace-level limit shared across connections and scaled to plan; 429 with `rate_limited` on breach. No paid upgrade path below Business/Enterprise (up to 100 rps by sales request). - **Pagination is recursive**: `blocks.children` returns only first-level children; you must check `has_children` and recurse, and *every level is independently paginated*. A single content-rich page can be 30+ requests. - **Payload limits**: 1000 block elements and 500 KB per request; rich text 2000 chars; equation expressions 1000 chars; block arrays 100 elements. - **The image killer**: every Notion-hosted file URL is an AWS S3 **signed URL carrying `expiry_time`, valid ~1 hour**. Notion's own guidance: regenerate from the block. So a statically-built page that hardcodes them starts 403-ing within the hour. Every build must download the bytes inside the signing window and re-host (locally or to R2). None of this is unsolvable; all of it is unnecessary complexity for an author who doesn't use Notion. --- ## 4. Hosted blogging / newsletter platforms - **Substack** — instantly recognisable chrome, surrenders the domain identity and typography. Fine as a *cross-post* with `rel=canonical` back to satishregonda.in; wrong as the home. (Substack's own pricing page 404'd on fetch; treat specific fee/cut numbers as UNVERIFIED.) - **Ghost(Pro)** — $18/mo Starter (own site, free custom domain, 1 newsletter, 1,000 members), $29/mo Publisher. Full Content API for headless on all plans, native newsletters on every tier. Genuinely good — but it's a whole CMS, and we already own a bespoke frontend. Paying $216/yr to *not* use most of it is the wrong trade. - **Medium** — no. - **Hashnode headless** — was the free headless option; as of **11 June 2026** the free plan is one publication on a `hashnode.dev` subdomain, with custom domains, the GraphQL API, headless mode, webhooks and GitHub backup all behind Hashnode Pro at $5/mo (pre-existing custom domains grandfathered). *This date/detail comes from a third-party guide and Hashnode's own pricing page didn't surface tier breakdowns on fetch — treat as UNVERIFIED, but the direction of travel is clear.* Either way it puts a third-party account between him and his own writing. - **Buttondown** — the right shape: **RSS-to-email**, "automatically send your subscribers a new email every time you publish a new blog post", multiple feeds combinable, schedulable weekly/monthly. Free to 100 subscribers (unlimited sends, custom domain, RSS, basic analytics); $9/mo to 1,000 (branding removal, API, automations). No revenue cut. **Should the blog also be a newsletter?** Yes — eventually, and only as a *derivative*. A hydrology/climate academic's audience (students, collaborators, agency contacts, journalists) is exactly the population that subscribes to things and never checks a website twice. But: ship the blog first, let 5–10 posts accumulate, then point Buttondown at `/rss.xml`. Building the email layer before there's a publishing habit is the classic way to end up with neither. --- ## 5. Markdown/MDX in the repo + preview deploy `github.dev` (press `.` on any repo, or swap `.com`→`.dev`) is free, runs entirely in-browser, gives search, syntax highlighting, Markdown preview, and a source-control view for commits. It is genuinely capable. It is still not viable as the primary surface for this author. The friction isn't the editor — it's the *conceptual model*: branch, stage, commit message, push, wait, check. Every one of those is a place where a professor writing his third post of the year will stop and email us instead. Add YAML frontmatter (where a stray colon in a title breaks the build) and the failure rate goes to near-certainty. Keep it as **our** editing surface, and as the documented emergency path for him with a screenshot walkthrough. It closes the gap for a one-character typo fix, not for authoring. --- ## 6. RECOMMENDED PIPELINE, END TO END **Where he writes.** Google Docs. Drive layout: ``` Website/ Blog/ Drafts/ ← writes here Published/ ← drags here to publish Retired/ ← drags here to unpublish data/ ← CSVs for charts ``` **How he marks a post ready.** He drags the Doc from `Drafts/` into `Published/`. Optionally opens Website → Publish this post from the Docs menu to skip the wait. **What runs.** `sync-blog.yml` on `*/15 * * * *` + `workflow_dispatch` + `repository_dispatch`: 1. Auth to Drive (service account; folder shared with `blog-bot@…iam.gserviceaccount.com` as Viewer). 2. `files.list` in `Published/`, `fields=files(id,name,createdTime,modifiedTime)`, `supportsAllDrives=true`. 3. `files.export(fileId, 'text/markdown')`; on `exportSizeLimitExceeded` (or >7 MB) retry with `application/zip`. 4. Normalize (§1.4, seven ordered steps). 5. Parse the leading "Post settings" pipe-table into frontmatter; delete it from the body. 6. Look up `_registry.json[fileId]` → reuse `slug` + `pubDate`, or stamp them now. Set `updatedDate` if the content hash moved. 7. Write `src/content/blog//index.md` + sibling images; downscale >2000px, WebP q82. 8. `npm run build`. **Only on success**, commit + push to `main`. 9. On failure: open/update a GitHub Issue and email one plain-English sentence. **How long until it's live.** ≤15 min unattended; ~90 s via the button; plus ~1–3 min Cloudflare Pages build. Call it "within twenty minutes, usually two." **On failure.** The site is untouched because the commit never happens. He gets an email naming the Doc and the problem in prose. **Typo after publishing.** Edit the Doc; that's all. Slug and pubDate are frozen in the registry; `updatedDate` moves; "Updated " appears only if >24h after publication. **Images.** Sync-side downscale + WebP; Astro `astro:assets` + sharp emits AVIF/WebP with `srcset` at build (build-time for prerendered pages, cached in `./node_modules/.astro`). Remote images would need `image.domains`/`image.remotePatterns` — we don't use remote images, so this doesn't apply. **Drafts private.** By construction — `Drafts/` is never read. No preview URL exists to leak. **Date and slug.** Stamped once into `_registry.json` on first appearance in `Published/`; `Date` and `Slug` rows in the settings table can override at creation only. **RSS.** `@astrojs/rss` → `/rss.xml`; `site` configured; full HTML via `content`, sanitized with `sanitize-html`, paths absolutised; `` in head. **Fallbacks, in order.** 1. Press Publish again. 2. Action failed → site unaffected, email sent, we fix. 3. Google changes the markdown export → flip a flag to the zip/HTML extractor (verified stable, real image files). 4. Total Google failure → edit the same markdown in **Sveltia CMS at `/admin`** with a GitHub PAT, from any device including his phone. --- ## 7. Content ergonomics — how each capability survives Google Docs | Capability | How he does it | How it survives | |---|---|---| | **Figure captions** | Insert image, then one all-italic line under it; fill the Alt text field | VERIFIED: alt text survives to `![alt][imageN]`; normalizer promotes the italic paragraph to `

exemplars.name: Lilian Weng — Lil'Log (OpenAI, personal research blog)
exemplars.what_works: Hugo + PaperMod. Chronological listing with pagination; every entry carries date, estimated reading time and author line. LaTeX renders inline in body prose ($L$, $N$, $D$). RSS in the footer. Keyboard shortcuts (Alt+H home, Alt+/ search, Alt+G top). Dedicated tags page rather than tag clutter on the index.
exemplars.steal_this: Estimated reading time on the index. For long-form hydrology explainers it sets expectations honestly, costs nothing to compute from the markdown, and is the single cheapest signal that a post is a real piece of writing rather than a news blurb.

exemplars.name: RealClimate — working climate scientists' group blog
exemplars.what_works: WordPress. Author bylines are first-class and link to author archives; comment counts sit next to titles; a 'Featured Story' slot elevates one piece above the feed; recurring monthly 'Unforced Variations' open threads give the blog a rhythm independent of research output.
exemplars.steal_this: The recurring-format post. A standing series — 'Monsoon Watch', say, posted at onset and withdrawal each year — gives an infrequent academic author a reason to publish that doesn't depend on having a finished idea. It converts 'I should blog sometime' into a calendar entry.

exemplars.name: EGU Hydrological Sciences Division Blog
exemplars.what_works: Directly in-domain. Every post opens with a captioned field photograph with explicit photo credit ('Sampling eDNA… Padastertal, Austria in September 2022 © Yvonne Schadewell'). Topic tags are discipline-native (Groundwater, Extreme Events, Teaching) rather than generic. Clickable author archives; explicit open call for contributions.
exemplars.steal_this: The credited, captioned field photo as the standard opening image. Hydrology work produces these constantly (gauges, floods, instruments, field campaigns) — it's free, authentic visual material that no template site can fake, and the credit line signals a working scientist rather than a stock-photo CMS.

exemplars.name: Nicholas Carlini — academic personal site
exemplars.what_works: Top nav splits Main / Papers / Talks / Code / Writing — peer-reviewed output is structurally separated from blog writing, so neither dilutes the other. Homepage runs a curated 'Selected Recent Work' rather than a raw reverse-chronological dump. Minimal graphics, academic typographic restraint, footnotes used inline in prose.
exemplars.steal_this: Papers and Writing as separate top-level destinations, with a hand-curated 'Selected' strip on the homepage instead of an auto-generated latest-N feed. It lets the professor foreground a 2019 paper that still matters over a 2026 post that doesn't.

exemplars.name: Simon Willison's Weblog
exemplars.what_works: Distinct content types — Entries, Links, Quotations, Notes, Guides — rendered differently, so a two-line link post and a 3,000-word analysis coexist without either feeling wrong. Tag frequency shown on the homepage. Archive browsable by year back to 2002. Atom feed at /atom/everything/.
exemplars.steal_this: The Entry-vs-Link distinction. It removes the biggest psychological barrier to infrequent blogging — the belief that every post must be an essay. A 'Link' type (one paragraph + an outbound URL) lets him post about a new HESS paper or an IMD forecast update in ninety seconds, which is what actually sustains a blog.

exemplars.name: Ben Recht — arg min (Substack)
exemplars.what_works: Serious academic writing on a custom domain with Substack doing delivery; prominent subscribe affordance; clear single-author identity with a stated editorial premise ('a blog of minimum value. on the history, foundations, and validity of "optimally" automated decision making').
exemplars.steal_this: The one-line stated premise under the blog title. It tells a reader in ten words what this blog is for and, more usefully, tells the author what to write. Worth writing before a single post exists — and it's exactly the kind of editorial decision that stops a site reading as generated.

pitfalls: Shipping the Google Docs pipeline WITHOUT the unescape normalizer. Everything will look fine in testing on prose-only posts, then the first post with an equation or a footnote renders as `$\\alpha \= \\beta^2$` and `\[^1\]`. This is the single most likely way this project embarrasses itself.

Deriving the slug from the Doc title on every sync. He will rename 'Monsoon onset 2026' to 'Monsoon onset over the Godavari, 2026' three weeks after publishing, the URL will change, and every inbound link and the Google index will break silently. Freeze slug + pubDate in a committed registry keyed by Drive fileId.

Deleting the markdown when a Doc disappears from Published/. Docs get moved by accident, and Drive's trash is not a rollback for your repo. Set `draft: true` and keep the file; never destroy content in response to an absence.

Putting the content repo on PUBLIC GitHub. Scheduled workflows in public repos are auto-disabled after 60 days without repository activity — which is exactly the cadence of an academic blog. The sync will stop and nobody will notice for months.
Using `cron: '0 * * * *'`. GitHub explicitly warns the schedule event is delayed at peak load and 'high load times include the start of every hour'. Use an offset like `*/15` or `7,22,37,52`.

Building a PR-review or staging-approval step 'for safety'. A non-technical author will not merge a PR. Posts will accumulate in an open-PR limbo and he will conclude the website is broken. The build-before-commit gate provides the safety without asking him for an action.

Committing raw phone-camera images from Docs into the repo. Google re-encodes on export but does not resize; a few field photos will bloat the repo and slow every subsequent build. Downscale and re-encode in the sync step, before git ever sees them.

Relying on `files.export` for image-heavy posts without handling the 10 MB cap. Base64 adds ~33%, so ~7 MB of real images breaks it. Detect and fall back to `application/zip` automatically — don't wait for a support email.

Using the Google Docs API's `inlineObjects[].contentUri` to fetch images. It has a documented 30-minute lifetime and is tagged to the requesting account, so it fails in exactly the intermittent, hard-to-reproduce way that costs a day of debugging. Use the export endpoints.

Choosing Decap CMS because it is the name everyone recognises. Its no-GitHub-account path depends on Git Gateway, which Netlify has deprecated and will no longer fix bugs in, and a moderate-severity XSS reported in Sept 2025 was reportedly still unpatched [UNVERIFIED — secondary source]. If a git CMS is wanted, it should be Sveltia.

Making Substack the home of the blog. It hands away the domain, the typography and the canonical URL, and Substack's chrome is so recognisable that the site would read as a template — the exact failure mode the brief forbids.

Wiring up Notion because it looks like the tidy modern answer. The 1-hour S3 signed-URL expiry on every image means a static build breaks within the hour unless you download and re-host everything, and 3 req/s with recursively paginated nested blocks makes even that slow.

Assuming Google Docs' Insert → Equation will work. The gd2md-html add-on's own documentation says Docs equations raise an alert and require manual MathJax/LaTeX conversion. Teach `$…$` from day one; never let him discover the equation editor.

Depending on fenced code blocks surviving a Doc. Verified: they do not — the fence is silently dropped and the contents come back as escaped paragraphs. If a post needs code, it needs the 1×1-table convention.

Writing the Astro markdown config against `markdown.remarkPlugins` / `rehypePlugins` / `gfm` / `smartypants`. All five are already marked deprecated and slated for removal; use `markdown.processor` now rather than rewriting the KaTeX setup in a year.

Building the newsletter before the blog has a publishing habit. Set up RSS properly, ship 5–10 posts, then point Buttondown at the feed. Launching an empty newsletter is how you end up with neither a list nor a blog.

Assuming the service-account + shared-folder approach will just work on iith.ac.in. A Workspace admin may block external sharing or Apps Script external requests. Design the Drive fetcher behind an interface so it can be swapped for an Apps-Script-Web-App source without touching the rest of the sync, and confirm the constraint during setup rather than at launch.

Giving him more than three or four authoring conventions. Every extra directive, shortcode or special table is a rule he will forget between posts published six months apart. The house-style card must fit on one side of one page.
